title: Hardening the object store that holds my Terraform state
summary: Every Terraform run in my lab reads its state from one S3-compatible store. I made it safe to rotate, rebuild and manage from code without moving that state.

stat.label: holds the state for every environment, so every change to it gets checked twice

sections.heading: Problem
paragraphs: The state for my infrastructure lives in a MinIO bucket that stands in for S3. It is versioned and uses native locking. But the store itself was configured by hand, one credential had been exposed, and the Ansible role that was supposed to describe it no longer matched the running host. Running that role on the live machine would have repointed the state backend.

sections.heading: What I did
paragraphs: First, a script rotates the exposed root credential and records the new one in the secrets store. Its first version rolled back every time, because its health check called a tool that the host does not have. A pull request switched the check to a language the host does have, and the rotation now holds.
Second, I found the vendor download site returns Gone for the pinned binary, so rebuilding the host from scratch would have failed. The role now fetches its binaries from a release in my own mirror.

Third, I made the role describe the running host exactly: its service account, environment file, service unit layout and firewall setting. A dry run with diffs is how I found each mismatch, and I fixed them one pull request at a time until the diff was clean. Other hosts keep the role's normal defaults.

sections.heading: Why this order
paragraphs: The goal was a role I could trust to rebuild the machine, not a role I would run and hope. Changing the state store is the one change that can lock me out of changing everything else, so I did not apply anything until the dry run showed nothing would change.

sections.heading: Lesson
paragraphs: A configuration role that has drifted from reality is worse than none, because it looks like documentation and acts like a command. Make it match what is running, prove it with a dry run, and then it becomes a safe path to a rebuild.
